headline: Yubi is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *oyonpE.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *oyonpE.

headline: Heiwa is a rearrangement of 和平 (wahei, “peace”), first attested in the Meiji era.

sources.quote: Rearrangement of 和平 (wahei, “peace”), likely that 平 (hei) also means "flat", therefore switching the kanji meant "calm, equal + harmony → peace".
First attested in the Meiji era.

headline: Mimau is 見 (mi) plus 舞う (mau).

sources.quote: 見(み) (mi) + 舞(ま)う (mau)

headline: Bussō is a pseudo-loan from Chinese, a reformation of 物騒がしい (monosawagashii).

sources.quote: Pseudo-loan from Chinese, a reformation of 物(もの)騒(さわ)がしい (monosawagashii, na-adjective). Alternatively, from 物忩(ぶっそう) (bussō).

meaning: to hold something in the mouth
headline: Kuwaeru is from Classical Japanese 咥ふ (kufafu), possibly related to 食う (kuu, “to eat; to grab with one's mouth”).

sources.quote: From Classical Japanese 咥(くは)ふ (kufafu). Possibly related to 食(く)う (kuu, “to eat; to grab with one's mouth”, historical form 食(く)ふ (kufu)), with auxilliary verb ふ (-fu), expressing repetition or ongoing state.

headline: Kazoku is from Middle Chinese 家族, but is not attested until 1808, so possibly a borrowing from modern written Chinese.

sources.quote: Ultimately from Middle Chinese 家族 (MC kae dzuwk). However, not attested until 1808, so possibly a borrowing from modern written Chinese 家族 (jiāzú) with the expected Japanese reading applied.

sources.quote: Compound of 規(き) (ki, “compass”) + 準(じゅん) (jun, “spirit level”).

headline: Kyū, “urgent”, is from Middle Chinese 急 (MC kip), and went through three sound changes.

sources.quote: /kipʉ/ → /kiɸʉ/ → /kiu/ → /kʲɨː/
From Middle Chinese 急 (MC kip).

headline: Dai, “title”, is from Middle Chinese 題.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 題 (MC dej|dejH).

headline: Kurashi is the continuative stem of 暮らす (kurasu, “to live, to lead a life”).

sources.quote: From 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 暮(く)らす (kurasu, “to live, to lead a life”).

meaning: to state, to express, to mention
headline: Noberu is from the classical lower bigrade verb のぶ (nobu), cognate with 伸べる (noberu) and 延べる (noberu).

sources.quote: From the classical lower bigrade verb (バ行下二段活用) のぶ (nobu). Cognate with Japanese 伸(の)べる (noberu) and 延(の)べる (noberu).

headline: Dakedo is だ (da, auxiliary expressing certainty) plus けど (kedo, “although”), first cited to 1907.

sources.quote: Compound of だ (da, auxiliary expressing certainty) + けど (kedo, “although”).
Historically, also analyzed as a clipping of だけれども (da keredomo).
First cited to 1907.

headline: Yopparai is the continuative stem of 酔っ払う (yopparau).

sources.quote: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 酔(よ)っ払(ぱら)う (yopparau).

headline: Shimau is from the root shim-, cognate with 締む (shimu, “to fasten, tighten”) and 閉まる (shimaru, “to be closed”).

sources.quote: From root shim-, cognate with classical verb 締む (shimu, “to fasten, tighten”) and modern verb 閉まる (shimaru, “to be closed”) + ふ (fu, auxiliary verb indicating repetition or ongoing action).

headline: Usagi is from Proto-Japonic *osanki, possibly cognate with Goguryeo 烏斯含 (*osegam), and “highly likely a regional Wanderwort”.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *osanki, variant of *wosanki. Possibly cognate with Goguryeo *烏斯含 (*osegam).It is highly likely a regional Wanderwort.

headline: Moshimoshi is a reduplication of もし (moshi), a shortened form of 申し (mōshi), from 申す (mōsu, “to speak”, humble).

sources.quote: Reduplication of もし (moshi), a shortened form of 申(もう)し (mōshi, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 申(もう)す (mōsu, “to speak”, humble)).

headline: En began as wen, from Middle Chinese 圓 (“circle”); the yen sense came in the Meiji period from 銀圓 (yínyuán), “round silver object(s)”.

sources.quote: /wen/ → /eɴ/
From Middle Chinese 圓 (MC hjwen), with the original sense of "circle, roundness".

The yen sense came much later in the Meiji period, from Chinese 圓 /圆 (yuán), itself from 銀圓 /银圆 (yínyuán, “round silver object(s), especially a piece of eight”). Compare Chinese 元 (yuán, “yuan”) and Korean 원 (won, “Korean won”). Doublet of 元 (gen, “yuan (Chinese currency)”), ユアン (yuan, “yuan (Chinese currency)”), and ウォン (won, “won (Korean currency)”).
The yen became the official currency of Japan in 1871, succeeding the 両(りょう) (ryō) and the 文(もん) (mon).

headline: Kaisuiyoku is 海水 (kaisui, “seawater”) plus 浴 (yoku, “bathing”).

sources.quote: 海水(かいすい) (kaisui, “seawater”) + 浴(よく) (yoku, “bathing”)

headline: Mizugi is 水 (mizu, “water”) plus 着 (-gi, “wear, clothes”), first attested in 1908.

sources.quote: 水(みず) (mizu, “water”) + 着(ぎ) (-gi, “wear, clothes”).
The ki changes to gi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
First attested in 1908.

headline: Saji was originally 茶 (sa, “tea”, the Tang reading) plus 匙 (ji, “spoon, scoop”), then re-interpreted as kun'yomi.

sources.quote: Originally a compound of 茶 (sa, “tea”, the tōon or Tang reading) + 匙 (ji, “spoon, scoop”). This on'yomi reading for a two-character term was then applied to the single-character 匙 spelling, and re-interpreted as kun'yomi.

headline: Sabaku, “desert”, was borrowed from Middle Chinese /*ʂamɑk̚/ as /*sabaku/.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese /*ʂamɑk̚/ > Japanese /*sabaku/.

headline: Gaku is from Middle Chinese 額 (MC ngaek).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 額 (MC ngaek).

meaning: expression of sympathy, expression of concern
headline: Mimai is the continuative stem of 見舞う (mimau), equivalent to 見 (mi) plus 舞い (mai).

sources.quote: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 見(み)舞(ま)う (mimau).
Equivalent to 見(み) (mi) + 舞(ま)い (mai, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 舞(ま)う (mau)).

headline: Kiiroi is 黄色 (kiiro) plus い (-i).

sources.quote: From 黄(き)色(いろ) (kiiro) + い (-i).

headline: Shokumotsu is Middle Chinese 食物, literally “eat + thing”, possibly altered from the goon reading jikimotsu.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 食物 (zyik mjut, literally “eat + thing”). Possible alteration from strict goon reading jikimotsu, changing goon jiki for kan'on shoku.

headline: Hyō is from Middle Chinese 表, attested in a portion of the Shoku Nihongi dated to 703.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 表 (MC pjiewX). Attested in a portion of the Shoku Nihongi dated to 703.

headline: Kan, “intuition”, is from Middle Chinese 勘 (MC khomH).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 勘 (MC khomH).

headline: Honnin is possibly from Middle Chinese, or composed in Japan from Sinitic elements, and is first cited to roughly 1215.

morphemes.meaning: main; real; the one under discussion

sources.quote: Possibly from Middle Chinese, or composed in Japan of Sinitic elements: 本 (hon, “main; real; the one under discussion”) + 人 (nin, “person”). Compare modern Mandarin 本人 (běnrén).
First cited to roughly 1215.
